## Did the statistical gate earn its cost?

Two selection rules, scored on the same held-out set:

| Rule | Chose | Validation | Held-out | Gap |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Statistical gate (this harness) | `standard+logreg` | 0.9741 | 0.9850 | -0.0109 |
| Greedy `max` (canonical loop) | `standard+logreg` | 0.9741 | 0.9850 | -0.0109 |

Both rules selected the same pipeline, so the gate cost nothing on this study. That is the common case when one configuration is clearly best; the gate matters when several are within noise of each other, which is when a greedy loop starts reporting inflated numbers.

## Protocol

- **Proposer:** heuristic
- **Validation:** repeated stratified k-fold, 15 fits per experiment, identical folds for every experiment (fixed seed) so comparisons are paired
- **Acceptance rule:** paired t-test at α=0.05, minimum effect 0.002
- **Held-out set:** scored exactly once, after the loop finished and the winner was fixed
- **Budget:** 12 experiments (12 evaluations used, 201.9s)
- **Seed:** 0

### Threats to validity

- One dataset and one study. The selection-rule comparison above is a single sample; `study.py --compare` repeats it across seeds.
- The held-out set is scored once, but it was split once too — a different split would move the final number by roughly its own standard error.
- The search space is fixed and declarative. The loop cannot invent a model family that is not in `search_space.py`, which is a deliberate safety boundary and a real ceiling on what it can discover.
